question:
You replace the embedding model in a RAG pipeline that passes the top 5 retrieved chunks to the generator. On a 200-question golden set, recall@10 rises from 0.78 to 0.84. Human-graded answer correctness barely moves: 61% to 62.5%. The team wonders if retrieval metrics 'don't matter'.

Give at least four distinct reasons this can happen, say how you would tell them apart with the data you already have, and what extra experiment establishes the ceiling on what better retrieval can deliver.
answer:
Recall@10 counts gold chunks in 10 positions, but the generator sees 5. Candidate explanations:

1. The gain sits at ranks 6-10. Recall@5 may not have moved at all. Always report recall at the k actually passed to the generator (and the rank distribution of the gold chunk).
2. The generator is the bottleneck. Many remaining failures happen with the right chunk in context: misreading, ignoring it, over-compressing, or hallucinating. Better retrieval cannot fix those.
3. The new hits are on questions the model already answered correctly from parametric knowledge, or on easy single-hop questions, while the hard ones (multi-hop, tables, negation) are unchanged.
4. Position and distraction effects: with long contexts, models often use evidence in the middle less reliably than at the edges, and extra irrelevant chunks can distract; a better embedder may reorder chunks without making the context cleaner.
5. Label problems: 'gold chunk retrieved' can overstate sufficiency (the chunk is relevant but incomplete, so the answer needs a second chunk) or the answer grader may be noisy.
6. Noise. A single 61% accuracy on n = 200 has a standard error of about 3.4 points, but for a before/after change on the same questions the relevant SE is about sqrt(number of flipped questions) / 200, for example 1.7 points if 11 questions flip (say 7 improved, 4 got worse). A net change of 3 questions (1.5 points) is within one standard error, so it says almost nothing alone.

Telling them apart: build a per-query transition table (retrieval hit before/after at the used k vs answer correct before/after) and look only at queries whose retrieval status changed. Check the rank of the gold chunk for the newly hit queries. Break results down by question type. Hand-read a sample of failures that have the gold chunk in context.

Ceiling experiment: run the generator with the gold chunk(s) injected as the context (oracle context). If correctness only rises to, say, the mid-70s, retrieval can at most close a limited gap and the generator or labels need attention; if oracle accuracy is far higher than current accuracy, retrieval and context assembly still have headroom. Also run a no-context baseline to measure parametric knowledge.

topic: RAG evaluation (recall@k, MRR, nDCG, faithfulness, golden sets, LLM judges)
question: Your retrieval golden set was built by annotators who judged only the top 10 results of the existing BM25 system for each query. You now evaluate a new dense retriever against it: its recall@10 and nDCG@10 come out lower than BM25's, yet when you read its results for 20 queries by hand, they look as good or better. Why can the metrics say this, and how would you fix the evaluation?
answer:
Recall, precision and nDCG all treat a document as relevant only if it appears in the judged-relevant set; unjudged documents count as non-relevant. When the labelled set came from the top 10 of BM25 only, relevant documents that BM25 cannot find were never shown to annotators, so they have no label. A dense retriever that surfaces such documents is penalised for exactly the behaviour you want, while BM25 is flattered because its own top results are the ones that got judged. This is pooling bias, and the metrics are biased towards systems similar to the one that built the pool.

Small example: the labelled relevant set for a query is {d1, d2, d3}. The dense system returns [d1, x, y, d2, z]. If x and y are truly relevant but never judged, measured recall@5 is 2/3 and precision@5 is 2/5, while the real precision@5 is 4/5 (if z is not relevant).

Diagnose it by computing the judged fraction at k (the share of each system's top-k that has any label). If BM25 is near 100% and the dense system is much lower, the comparison is unreliable. Also sample the unjudged dense results and have a human (or a carefully validated LLM judge) label them to estimate how many are relevant.

Fixes: (1) pool the top results from several different systems (BM25, dense, hybrid, the new candidate) before annotating, and re-pool when you add a new system; (2) judge the unjudged documents in the new system's top k, which is usually a small extra batch; (3) as a sensitivity check, report metrics on 'condensed lists' that drop unjudged documents; (4) keep the judged fraction as a standard column in every eval report; (5) when labels are partial, treat measured precision@k as a lower bound (unjudged hits count as misses); measured recall is biased too, but its denominator is also incomplete, so it is not a strict bound. More queries do not help because the missing labels bias every query in the same direction.

question:
Some of your RAG questions need several pieces of evidence (for example a policy rule plus its exception), and for each piece there may be several acceptable chunks because the corpus contains near-duplicates. Averaging plain recall@k over queries hides whether the generator actually receives everything it needs.

Implement evidence_coverage(ranked, groups, k), where groups is a list of sets of chunk ids and a group counts as covered if any of its chunks is in the top k, returning (fraction of groups covered, whether all groups are covered), and aggregate(runs, k) returning (mean coverage, full-coverage rate). Here runs is a list of (ranked, groups) pairs. Use these four queries: (1) ranked [c1, c9, c2, c7], groups [{c1}, {c2, c20}]; (2) [c5, c3, c8, c4], [{c3}, {c6}]; (3) [c10, c11], [{c12}]; (4) [c1, c2, c3, c4], [{c4}, {c3}, {c40}]. Explain why mean coverage and full-coverage rate move differently when k goes from 3 to 4.
answer:
Plain recall@k averages over gold chunks. For a question that needs two chunks, retrieving one of them gives recall 0.5 but usually gives a generator that cannot answer correctly, because the second piece (the exception, the second hop) is missing. What matters for answerability is whether all required pieces are present, so report both: mean coverage (partial credit, a smooth signal for tuning) and the full-coverage rate (the share of questions whose evidence is complete, closer to the answer-correctness ceiling).

Modelling evidence as groups of acceptable chunks handles duplicates and overlapping chunk boundaries: a group is covered if any member is retrieved, so retrieving the equivalent duplicate is not penalised, and several retrieved duplicates of the same group count once (a chunk listed in two groups would cover both, so keep groups disjoint). Define the groups when building the golden set (by pooling and judging, not just by the chunk the question came from).

In the four-query example, at k = 3 the per-query coverages are 1.0, 0.5, 0.0 and 1/3, so mean coverage is 0.458, and only the first query is fully covered (rate 0.25). Going to k = 4 raises the fourth query to 2/3 and mean coverage to 0.542, but the full-coverage rate stays at 0.25, because the second query still misses its second group and the fourth has a group (c40) that is nowhere in the ranking. A larger k can look like progress on the mean while giving the generator no more complete evidence sets. Note too that a larger k means more context tokens and more distractors for generation.

Caveats: coverage says nothing about rank order (pair it with MRR or nDCG), about whether the chunk is sufficient on its own, or about whether the generator uses it. Edge cases: no groups is an invalid question (unanswerable questions need their own handling), and k = 0 gives zero coverage.

def evidence_coverage(ranked, groups, k):
    """ranked: list of chunk ids. groups: list of sets; a group is covered if ANY of
    its chunk ids is in the top-k. Returns (fraction of groups covered, all covered)."""
    if not groups:
        raise ValueError("a question needs at least one evidence group")
    top = set(ranked[:k]) if k > 0 else set()
    covered = sum(1 for g in groups if g & top)
    return covered / len(groups), covered == len(groups)

    n = len(res)
    return sum(c for c, _ in res) / n, sum(1 for _, ok in res if ok) / n

topic: Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
question:
A 20M-chunk collection sits in an HNSW index. Queries always carry a metadata filter. For a filter such as department='legal' AND year=2019, only about 0.5% of vectors match (roughly 100,000 chunks). With ef_search=100 and top_k=10, the service often returns only 0 to 2 results, though the same query unfiltered returns 10 sensible hits and an exact scan with the filter returns 10 good ones.

Explain why this happens with post-filtering, what in-graph (filtered) traversal and pre-filtering change, and how you would choose a strategy by selectivity.
answer:
Post-filtering: the index returns the ef_search nearest candidates ignoring the filter, then the engine discards non-matching ones. If the filter is roughly independent of the query, the expected number of survivors is ef_search x selectivity = 100 x 0.005 = 0.5, far below top_k = 10. To get 10 survivors on average you would need ef around 2,000 (10 / 0.005), which costs latency and still fails when the filter correlates with the query (a query about a topic that lies mostly outside 'legal 2019' will rarely have matching items among its nearest neighbours). Raising top_k does not help for the same reason.

Pre-filtering with exact scan: evaluate the filter first (inverted index or bitmap), giving about 100,000 ids, then compute exact distances for just those. For 768-d float32 vectors that is about 100,000 x 768 x 4 bytes = 307 MB of vector data to read, acceptable for a rare query pattern and perfect recall within the filter, but too heavy at high QPS or when the filter passes millions of vectors.

Traversal-time (in-graph) filtering: search the graph but only admit matching nodes to the result set, in some engines still walking through non-matching nodes and in others restricting the walk to matching ones. It works well for moderate selectivity, but when matching nodes are very sparse, the search wanders through mostly non-matching regions, the effective graph of matching nodes can become disconnected, and recall or latency degrades; implementations differ in how they handle this (for example by switching to a brute-force path when the filter is selective enough).

Partitioning: if a few filter fields are used on nearly every query (tenant, year, language), build separate indexes or partitions per value so that the ANN index only holds eligible vectors.

Choosing: estimate selectivity per query from filter statistics; use post-filter with generous ef when most data matches (for example more than half); use traversal-time filtering in the middle range; use pre-filter plus exact scan when the matching set is small enough to scan within the latency budget. Always measure recall against an exact filtered search on a sample of real filter/query combinations, split by selectivity band, since average recall hides the selective cases.

topic: Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
question: You must serve 50 million chunks, 768-d float32 embeddings, from an in-memory HNSW index with M=16, with 3 replicas for availability and throughput. Each node has about 100 GB usable for the index. Estimate memory for the base design, work out how many nodes it needs, and compare it with int8 scalar quantisation and product quantisation with 96-byte codes. Which would you choose and what would you verify before deciding?
answer:
Assumptions (state them in the interview; real engines differ): decimal GB; layer 0 stores up to 2M = 32 neighbour ids of 4 bytes per node; upper layers add roughly n/(M-1) node-layer entries with up to M links each; per-node headers, ids, allocator overhead and metadata are ignored and typically add more.

Base design: vectors = 50e6 x 768 x 4 B = 153.6 GB. Layer-0 links = 50e6 x 32 x 4 B = 6.4 GB. Upper layers add about 0.2 GB. Total about 160.2 GB per full copy. Three replicas = about 480.6 GB cluster-wide.

Nodes: one copy does not fit within 100 GB, so shard it: ceil(160.2 / 100) = 2 shards of about 80 GB each, times 3 replicas = 6 nodes. Replicas multiply cost but not capacity.

int8 scalar quantisation: 1 byte per dimension gives 38.4 GB for vectors plus 6.6 GB for the graph = 45.0 GB per copy, which fits on one node, so 3 nodes with 3 replicas. The recall loss is often small but data- and model-dependent, so measure it.

Product quantisation with 96 one-byte codes per vector (8 dimensions per sub-vector): 4.8 GB + 6.6 GB = 11.4 GB per copy. Each copy fits on one node, so it still needs 3 nodes (the replica count is the floor), the same as int8; the gain is only that nodes could be much smaller. It is lossy: distances are approximate, so many setups re-rank the top candidates with full-precision vectors stored on SSD or in object storage (153.6 GB on disk), adding latency and I/O. The graph links, not the vectors, dominate once codes are this small.

topic: Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
question:
A RAG service re-ingests documents weekly; each document is split into chunks and upserted into an HNSW-based vector store, and deleted documents are removed with a 'delete by chunk id' call. Six months in, you see: memory and disk keep growing though the corpus is stable, p95 latency is creeping up, recall on a fixed monitoring set has dropped a little, and legal reports that a withdrawn document still appears in answers.

Explain the likely mechanisms and design the update and delete path properly.
answer:
Likely mechanisms:

1. Soft deletes. Many ANN implementations mark deleted vectors (tombstones) and filter them from results but leave them in the graph and storage until a compaction or rebuild. Memory and disk do not shrink; searches can still traverse deleted nodes, which may consume part of the ef budget (implementation-dependent; Qdrant documents graph disconnection with many soft-deleted points); and repeatedly inserting into a graph around deleted nodes can reduce graph quality. This fits growing memory, slower queries and mildly lower recall. Behaviour varies by engine, so check the one you use.
2. Orphaned chunks. If chunk ids are random per ingest, or are position-based (doc42_chunk_11) while a document shrinks from 12 to 9 chunks, then re-upserting by id overwrites some chunks and leaves chunks 10 to 12 of the old version alive. Edited text also shifts chunk boundaries, so the old and new versions coexist and the corpus quietly grows with stale, contradictory text.
3. The withdrawn document: the delete was keyed on chunk ids the pipeline no longer had (or ran before the index refresh made it visible), so some chunks survive.

Design: (a) store doc_id, doc_version and chunk ordinal as metadata, with chunk ids derived from doc_id and version; (b) update = write the new version, then delete everything for that doc_id with an older version (a delete-by-filter on doc_id, not a list of ids you remember); (c) add a query-time filter on an 'active' flag or valid_to timestamp so removals take effect for retrieval immediately even before physical deletion, which is what a compliance deletion needs; (d) monitor the deleted/live ratio and run compaction or a rebuild based on it, validating recall against an exact search on a held-out query set; (e) for large rebuilds build a new index in the background and switch an alias or pointer atomically, with the ability to roll back; (f) reconcile periodically: compare doc ids in the source of truth against the index and fix drift; (g) remember that other copies (caches, reranker caches, backups, answer logs) may also contain the withdrawn text.

topic: Vector databases and index operations (filters, freshness, updates, cost)
question:
Users of a news-assistant RAG product expect a newly published article to be answerable within about 30 seconds. Today the vector index is rebuilt every night, ingestion runs at roughly 200 new chunks per second at peak, and queries must stay under 200 ms at p95.

Design how new documents become searchable quickly without rebuilding the whole index, say where the 30 seconds actually go, and discuss the consistency and cost trade-offs.
answer:
Architecture: a main index (ANN, large, rebuilt or compacted in the background) and a delta/fresh segment that accepts writes. Ingestion path: document arrives, is queued, chunked, embedded (often a batched model call), written to a durable log, then added to the fresh segment. A query searches main and fresh in parallel and merges the two top-k lists by similarity (valid because both use the same embedding model and metric; for hybrid keyword scores, normalise or fuse by rank since term statistics differ across segments).

Fresh segment sizing: at 200 chunks per second, an hour accumulates 720,000 chunks. Brute-forcing 768-d float32 vectors for that many chunks means reading about 720,000 x 768 x 4 B = 2.2 GB per query, which is too heavy at high QPS if you let the segment grow for an hour. So flush frequently: after, say, a few minutes (tens of thousands of chunks, tens of MB to a few hundred MB per scan, depending on the interval), convert the segment to a small ANN index or keep it exact, and start a new fresh segment. Many segments increase query fan-out and tail latency, so a background compaction merges small segments into larger ones, in the style of log-structured merge designs.

Where the 30 seconds go: measure end to end. Message-queue delay, fetching and cleaning documents, chunking, the embedding call (rate limits and batching delays), the index refresh interval (a newly written vector is often invisible until the next refresh or commit), and replication to read replicas. Optimising index internals will not help if embedding batches wait 20 seconds to fill.

Trade-offs: a shorter refresh interval gives fresher results but creates more tiny segments and write amplification; read-your-writes consistency for the publishing user may need a routing hint or a direct lookup; deletes and updates must be applied to both main and fresh segments (see tombstone handling); recall of ANN on the main index is not the same as exact scan on the fresh one, but that mismatch is usually acceptable; and failures need a durable log so the fresh segment can be rebuilt after a crash. Nightly rebuilds then become compaction jobs rather than the freshness mechanism.

question:
A SaaS RAG product serves 3,000 tenants. Sizes are heavily skewed: most have a few hundred chunks, a handful have millions. Candidate designs: (a) one shared index with a tenant_id filter, (b) a separate index per tenant, (c) a hybrid. Customers require that one tenant can never retrieve another's data, and that deleting a tenant removes all its vectors.

Compare the designs on isolation, search quality and latency, cost, noisy neighbours and erasure, and say which you would build.
answer:
(a) Shared index with a tenant_id filter. Cheapest for many small tenants and simple to operate, but: isolation depends on every query path adding the filter, so one missing clause is a cross-tenant leak; a tenant with 300 chunks among 100M has selectivity around 3e-6, so post-filtered ANN returns nothing or poor results (see filtered-ANN behaviour) unless the engine pre-filters or scans exactly; one heavy tenant's queries or ingestion can consume shared capacity (noisy neighbour); deleting a tenant means many deletes with tombstones, compaction and no hard proof of removal.

(b) One index (or collection) per tenant. Strong logical isolation, per-tenant tuning, simple erasure (drop the index) and the ability to place a large tenant on its own hardware. But fixed overhead per index (memory, file handles, background threads, cluster metadata) multiplies by thousands, and tiny tenants waste it. Engines differ in how many indexes they handle well, so test your own.

(c) Hybrid, which I would choose. Tier 1: very small tenants (a few hundred to a few thousand chunks) live in shared partitions keyed by tenant. At that size an exact scan within the tenant's partition is cheap (a few hundred 768-d vectors is trivial) and avoids ANN recall problems entirely. Tier 2: large tenants get dedicated indexes or shards, so they are isolated, tuned and scaled independently; a tenant graduates when its size or traffic passes a threshold. A routing layer maps tenant to location.

Isolation controls beyond the filter: derive the tenant from the authenticated token in a gateway, not from user input; make the data layer enforce scoping (per-tenant namespaces, row-level policies, or credentials limited to a tenant's collection) so a forgotten filter cannot cross tenants; test with canary documents per tenant and automated cross-tenant queries; include tenant id in cache keys for retrieval and generation caches; consider per-tenant encryption keys where regulations demand. Erasure: dedicated index drops cleanly; shared partitions need delete-by-tenant plus compaction and a verification query; remember backups, logs and caches.

Monitor per-tenant latency and size, set rate limits per tenant, and automate promotion between tiers.

question:
A hybrid search service runs BM25 and dense retrieval across 8 shards. Each shard computes BM25 with its own local statistics, returns its top 20, and the coordinator merges the lists by raw score and then fuses with the dense list. After the corpus was resharded unevenly, queries with rare terms started returning odd rankings, and the hybrid scores seem on a different scale than the dense ones.

Why does this happen, and how should the merging and fusion work?
answer:
Why raw merging fails: BM25 weights terms by IDF, computed from document frequency and collection size. Using the common Lucene-style form idf = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)), a term that appears in 5 of 250,000 documents on one shard has idf of about 10.72, while on another shard where it appears in 40 of 250,000 it has about 8.73. For the same term frequency and document length, the first shard produces larger scores. Merging by raw score then favours shards where the term happens to be locally rare, a bias that grows with uneven resharding (for example one shard holding a topical cluster). When the corpus was split randomly, local statistics approximate the global ones for common terms and the problem is usually small (very rare terms stay noisy even then); after skewed resharding it is not.

question: A RAG assistant answers 'What is the notice period for terminating the Enterprise plan?' with '30 days', but the policy says 60 days. Logging shows the correct policy chunk was retrieved at rank 2 and is in the prompt. Lay out a step-by-step triage to find out why the answer is wrong, with the experiment that separates each cause.
answer:
Retrieval recall is not the problem if the correct chunk is truly in the prompt (retrieval precision may still be), so the question is why the generator did not use it correctly. Candidate causes and the discriminating checks:

1. A conflicting chunk is also in the prompt (for example an older policy or a different plan saying 30 days). Check: read the whole prompt, not just rank 2. If another chunk says 30 days, this is a retrieval/versioning problem after all (stale or wrong-plan chunk), and the fix is filtering by version or plan.
2. The chunk is present but the relevant sentence is truncated, mangled by extraction or separated from its table header (so '60' is not attached to 'Enterprise'). Check: print the exact chunk text as the model saw it.
3. Parametric override: the model answers from memory or from a common default ('30 days' is a typical notice period) instead of the context. Check: run the same prompt with the chunk removed; if the answer is still '30 days', that value comes from the model's prior or from another chunk, so the gold chunk is not what drives the answer; also run with only the correct chunk. If it then answers 60, distractors are the problem; if it still answers 30 with only the gold chunk, the model is overriding or misreading the context (see 6).
4. Position or distraction effects with many chunks: move the chunk to the first position and reduce k. A model-dependent effect, so test.
5. Prompt instructions that allow or encourage outside knowledge, or conflict (for example 'be concise' leading to dropping conditions). Check: re-run with a strict 'answer only from the context, say not found otherwise' instruction and compare.
6. Reasoning or reading error on a complex clause ('60 days, or 30 days for plans under 10 seats'): the model took the wrong branch. Check: ask for the supporting quote; if the quote is correct but the conclusion is wrong, it is a reasoning failure.

Run these as controlled ablations on the failing example and then on a set of similar failures, since one example can mislead. The measure that separates generation from retrieval is faithfulness/correctness conditional on the gold chunk being supplied: if accuracy is high with the gold chunk alone and low with the production context, the context assembly is at fault.

question: Answers are fluent and confident, but spot checks show many sentences are not in any retrieved chunk. Some are true, some are wrong. How do you determine whether the model is drawing on its own training knowledge, over-generalising from the chunks, or being fed irrelevant context, and what does each finding imply for the fix?
answer:
'Unsupported' is a property of claim versus context; the causes differ in where the claim came from, so the first step is to measure support at claim level, then run tests that vary the context.

Step 1: split answers into atomic claims and label each as supported, contradicted or not found in the provided context (human labels on a sample, or a calibrated entailment judge). This gives the unsupported-claim rate, and shows whether unsupported claims are mostly true (suggesting parametric knowledge or sensible inference) or mostly wrong (confabulation or over-generalisation).

Step 2: closed-book test. Ask the same questions with no retrieved context. If the unsupported claims in the RAG answer reappear in the closed-book answer, they come from the model's parametric knowledge. Fix: stronger instructions to answer only from context, a requirement to cite per claim, an abstain option, and possibly a verifier that removes unsupported claims.

Step 3: relevance test. Measure whether the retrieved chunks actually contain the answer (context recall against a labelled answer span, or a manual check of 30 cases). If answer-bearing text is absent, the model fills gaps because the question cannot be answered from its context; the fix is retrieval, plus abstention when evidence is weak.

Step 4: over-generalisation test. When the answer-bearing text is present but the output states more than it says (a rule extended to all regions, a number rounded or merged), check the claim against the cited quote. Fix: quote-first prompting, lower generation temperature (helps variability, not the cause), and a verifier step.

Interpretation caution: a true but unsupported claim is still a policy risk when the system promises answers 'from the documents', and the correct fraction does not make the system faithful. The metrics to report are faithfulness (claims supported by context) separately from correctness (claims true), because the two diverge in exactly this scenario.

topic: RAG failure diagnosis
question: Offline, your RAG system scores recall@5 of 0.92 and faithfulness 0.95 on the golden set, yet thumbs-down feedback is high, and users say answers are 'not what I asked' or 'outdated'. List the plausible reasons offline metrics and user feedback disagree and the analysis you would run to find which applies.
answer:
The two signals measure different things, so the mismatch is informative.

Possible causes:
1. Query distribution shift. Golden queries are often written by the team, clean and well-formed; real users write short, vague, typo-laden, multi-part or follow-up queries ('what about for contractors?') that need conversation context. Retrieval and answers on those can be much worse.
2. Stale evaluation. The golden set labelled last quarter's corpus; new or changed documents are not represented, and 'outdated' complaints reflect freshness failures that offline sets cannot see.
3. Metric blind spots. Recall@5 shows the evidence was retrieved, not that the answer was complete or well-formed; faithfulness measures support, not usefulness: a faithful but evasive or overly narrow answer scores well. Answer relevance and completeness may not be tracked.
4. Coverage gaps. Users ask things the corpus cannot answer; the offline set may only include answerable questions, so abstention behaviour is untested.
5. Feedback bias. Unhappy users are more likely to click, and thumbs-down can reflect latency, tone, UI or a missing feature, not answer quality.
6. Judge or label issues: if faithfulness is scored by an LLM judge, it may be lenient and miscalibrated against humans.

Analysis: (a) sample 100 thumbs-down interactions and classify them (wrong retrieval, stale source, wrong intent, missing content, tone/format, unrelated to answer); (b) compare real query logs to the golden set by length, type, language and topic, and add a stratified slice of real queries (with consent and privacy handling) to the eval; (c) slice feedback rate by feature (conversation turn, doc type, age of source); (d) check whether the golden-set metrics predict feedback at the query level (do low-recall queries get more thumbs-down?). The change that comes out of it is usually a refreshed, production-sampled eval set, not a tweak to the model.

question: After a weekend re-index in which you also switched to a newer embedding model and changed chunk size from 512 to 256, answer quality drops and some previously working queries now fail. Without being able to blame one change by intuition, how do you isolate the cause, and what would you have done before the migration to make this easy?
answer:
Three changes were made at once: embedding model, chunk size, and (implicitly) a full re-ingest that may have altered parsing, filters or metadata. Isolate by changing one factor at a time against a fixed labelled query set, and do not rely on intuition about which factor is likely.

Isolation procedure:
1. Reproduce with a regression set: take queries that worked before (from logs or the golden set) and measure recall@k and answer quality on the old and new index. Identify the queries that regressed; patterns (long queries, identifiers, tables) hint at the cause.
2. Build a factor grid if the old index is still available: old model with 512 chunks (baseline), new model with 512, old model with 256, new model with 256. Compare each against baseline, scoring hits by whether a retrieved chunk contains the labelled answer span (chunk IDs differ across chunk sizes), and keep in mind that the same k covers half as much text at 256 tokens. Interactions matter too, and the new model may need a different query/document prefix or normalisation, and the embedding dimension or similarity metric may differ.
3. Check for plain bugs unrelated to the factors: query and document embedded by different model versions (a mixed index or an unchanged query encoder), wrong distance metric for the new model, missing normalisation, lost metadata fields so filters match nothing, a truncated input exceeding the new model's token limit, different parsing, or an incomplete index (count of chunks versus expectation).
4. Chunk size effect on the prompt: 256-token chunks double the chunk count per document, so the same top-k now covers half the text; if k and the context budget were not retuned, the model sees less evidence per query.
5. Verify end-to-end separately from retrieval, since a retrieval gain can still reduce answer quality.

Prevention: version the index (blue/green with an alias), keep the old index until the new one passes the regression set, change one thing per release, keep a frozen canary query set with expected sources, and log the model and chunker versions in the chunk metadata. Rolling back then takes one alias flip back to the old collection (alias changes are atomic), provided the old collection was kept.

Check for plain bugs unrelated to the factors: query and document embedded by different model versions (a mixed index or an unchanged query encoder), wrong distance metric for the new model, missing normalisation, lost metadata fields so filters match nothing, a truncated input exceeding the new model's token limit, different parsing, or an incomplete index (count of chunks versus expectation).
4. Chunk size effect on the prompt: 256-token chunks double the chunk count per document, so the same top-k now covers half the text; if k and the context budget were not retuned, the model sees less evidence per query.
5. Verify end-to-end separately from retrieval, since a retrieval gain can still reduce answer quality.

Prevention: version the index (blue/green with an alias), keep the old index until the new one passes the regression set, change one thing per release, keep a frozen canary query set with expected sources, and log the model and chunker versions in the chunk metadata. Rolling back then takes one alias flip back to the old collection (alias changes are atomic), provided the old collection was kept.

2x2 result table (hypothetical recall@5 on 400 regression queries):
old model / 512: 0.88
new model / 512: 0.90
old model / 256: 0.81
new model / 256: 0.83
Reading: the new model helps by about 2 points; the smaller chunks cost about 7 points at the same k. Next steps: either return to 512, or at 256 raise k to cover the same text and add parent-child context, and re-measure. Also confirm the 12 queries that now return nothing are not caused by missing metadata or input truncation (inspect their filters and token counts).

topic: RAG failure diagnosis
question: Users of an internal assistant complain that questions containing acronyms and IDs ('What does SLA-7 cover?', 'Status of ticket INC-48213?', 'Is DPA required?') get wrong or irrelevant answers, while natural-language questions work well. The system uses dense retrieval only. Explain why, how you would confirm the diagnosis with measurements, and the fixes in order of cost.
answer:
Why: a dense embedding encodes semantic similarity of text pieces learned from training data. Rare strings such as 'INC-48213' or a company-specific acronym are tokenised into subword fragments with little meaning, so their embeddings are plausibly weakly informative and may sit close to many other IDs (dense retrievers are documented to underperform sparse methods on entity-centric questions); 'SLA-7' may be close to 'SLA-8' or generic SLA text. Exact-match signals (BM25 or keyword search) handle these naturally because the token is rare and highly discriminative. Acronyms add ambiguity (DPA could mean data processing agreement or something else) which dense models may resolve using general-world knowledge, not your domain.

Confirm: (1) split the query log into identifier/acronym queries and others (regex for IDs, a dictionary for acronyms), compare recall@k on the labelled subset of each; (2) run BM25 or hybrid on the same subset and check whether recall jumps; (3) inspect the top results for failures: if near-miss IDs (SLA-8) appear, that is the embedding conflation signature; (4) for acronyms, check whether the chunk uses the long form only (so the acronym never appears in the text) or the reverse.

Fixes in order of cost:
1. Add lexical retrieval and fuse with dense (RRF or weighted fusion); cheap and usually effective for exact tokens. Make sure the analyser does not split or drop the ID format.
2. Query-side handling: detect IDs and route them to exact lookup in a structured store or metadata filter (ticket status belongs in a ticket API, not a document index).
3. Acronym expansion: glossary mapping applied to both queries and chunks at indexing time, or to the query by rewriting.
4. Domain adaptation: fine-tune the embedder with domain pairs; the highest cost and least certain, and it still handles arbitrary IDs poorly.

Also note that live-status questions like ticket state need live data, so the answer should come from a tool call rather than a stale index.
